#1954. GdS: Tactics, data and team-mates – the ‘strange case’ of Goncalo Ramos at Milan

The Goncalo Ramos enigma continues to dominate the newspaper columns, as AC Milan try unlock their record signing.

As La Gazzetta dello Sport report, Milan fans hoped they had finally found a top-class striker in Ramos, but his three goals this season are not sufficient compared to expectations and the €70m price tag for which he arrived.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

And yet, the Portuguese centre-forward is still proving to be a factor in the team’s fortunes. The reason for this lies behind statistics that the average fan might ignore, but Ruben Amorim certainly isn’t.

The coach has repeatedly emphasised how Ramos is helping the team, less so the other way around. Looking at the numbers, you can’t argue with him. Gonçalo may not be making it into the top scorers’ table, but his work is well explained by statistics that place him among the top strikers in Serie A.

Which ones? Passes (20.7 per game, first in volume among centre-forwards in the league ahead of Lazio’s Noslin) or touches (2nd), for example. But also the aerial duels won and fouls drawn (19, first among attackers) underscore the importance of his sacrifice too.

There are two considerations that don’t emerge from the statistics, but are equally important. The first concerns the movements that free up or facilitate team-mates, such as the sprint for Milan’s first goal in Genoa.

Alphadjo Cisse found himself all alone in the penalty area thanks to Ramos drawing two of the Rossoblu central defenders towards him, allowing Adrien Rabiot to easily pass to the young Italian who was in lots of space.

The second consideration concerns the pressure and coverage work, which has changed since the start of the season. In the early days, Gonçalo was the first to apply pressure up front, but in doing so, he exposed Modric to too much space to cover in front of or behind him.

Amorim therefore asked the Portuguese to instead harass the opposing playmaker, without attacking the defence in the initial possession. This move allows Luka to run less and think more during the opponent’s possession phase.

We were talking about a Milan side that is helping Ramos less than the centre-forward is helping the team, too. The former Benfica man is 19th in Serie A for shots (26) and 15th for shots on target (10).

While it’s true that the Rossoneri maintain a high standard in terms of the quality of chances created (third in the league for big chances behind Inter and Roma), it’s equally undeniable that they arrive in the final third of the pitch less often than expected. Milan are 12th for touches in the opponent’s penalty area and 12th for shots on target.

In short, Ramos sees the ball mostly where he can’t hurt the goalkeepers. Even if, in relation to goal-scoring chances, he should have scored double in the league: 4.16 xG compared to the just two scored. Still, not enough for a Milan-calibre player.

#1953. Eight big money exits Brighton will consider amid shock Liverpool and Manchester United claim

It will come as little surprise that Brighton's top players are in the transfer spotlight following their blistering start to the season.

The Seagulls are second in the Premier League after 10 matches with many experts now tipping Brighton to be Arsenal's closest title rivals.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

The challenge as always will be for the Seagulls to keep their best players but if Brighton do decide to sell. then the timing and the price has to be right.

Brilliant young centre back Luka Vuskovic was yesterday linked with a move a £80m summer move to Liverpool with transfer expert Florian Plettenberg stating that Vuskovic is on the shortlist at Anfield.

Here's the latest on Vuskovic and a seven other Brighton stars - including head coach Fabian Hurzeler - who are attracting transfer interest.

Luka Vuskovic: Brighton smashed their transfer record to sign the Croatian teenager from Tottenham for just under £50m last summer. Vuskovic has been superb in the early stages of his Brighton career and the BBC reported today that Liverpool are keen. Vuskovic though previously said his aim is to play in La Liga, so don't be surprised to see him at Real Madrid in future, he's that good. Brighton should double their money on their brilliant young centre back.

Bart Verbruggen: The Dutch international is currently playing the best football of his career and helped Brighton to seven clean sheets in the Premier League this season. Brighton signed Verbruggen for around £15m three years and he has developed into one of the most in-demand goalkeepers in world football. Real Madrid, Barcelona and Bayern Munich have previously been linked. The 23-year-old, speaking ahead of Albion's Conference League win in Getafe, said: "You never know what will happen in future, but I'm happy at Brighton."

Yasin Ayari: The Sweden international and Brighton have so far failed to agree on a new contract. The 23-year-old has been excellent for Brighton in the past few seasons and has - according to the BBC - attracted interest from Chelsea. Italian clubs are also said to monitering the situation. The 23-year-old is out of contract this summer but Brighton are said to have an option for a further year.

Yankuba Minteh: The flying Gambian is just getting back to full fitness after a leg injury. Liverpool made two bids of around £60m and £70m for the former Newcastle man last summer, which Brighton rejected. Minteh will have to prove his form and fitness in the second half the season and if he does, then expect further interest from Liverpool and perhaps other top clubs from the Premier League and across Europe.

Kaoru Mitoma: The Japan international is yet to feature this term as he recovers from a long term hamstring injury. The winger joined Brighton in 2021 for around £3m and proved himself to be one of the most dangerous wingers in the Premier League. The 29-year-old is out of contract this summer and could eye a move away if the offer is right. Many Brighton fans would be sorry to see him go. A unique talent.

Charalampos Kostoulas: The Greek teenager has made a huge impact this season with five goals and four assists in all competitions. Kostoulas joined Brighton in 2025 for around £30m and after a slow start, he's really started to find his form. His workrate is impressive, his finishing can be clinical and he's also capable of the spectacular. This week former England and Manchester United striker Teddy Sheringham was singing his praises and urged his former club Man United to sign him this summer.

Maxim De Cuyper: The Belgian international has perhaps been a surprise package this season. The left sided player has excelled in Mitoma's absence with four goals and four assists already this term. Brighton signed him for around £15m in 2025 and recent reports suggest Italian clubs Roma, AC Milan and Juventus are all keen, with a potential value of £60m.

Fabian Hurzeler: This adds another dynamic as the impressive young German head coach will no doubt be in high demand this summer. The 33-year-old has been hugely impressive for the Seagulls since arriving from St Pauli in 2024. Manchester United were previously linked with Hurzeler, who is now one of the most sought after young coaches in European football. He is under contract until June 2029 and Brighton will demand a hefty compensation package if a club tries to prise him away.

Whilst they named a strong side, Challinor basically wrote the game off, more interested in protecting his first-teamers from injury than using what was effectively the second of two pre-season games for him to decide his line-up for his first match that really matters – Plymouth Argyle at home on Saturday.

So it was no surprise Accrington ran out 4-0 winners, Josh Smith's goal added to by the Charlies – Brown, Warren and Caton.

When the final whistle blew, it felt like a missed opportunity to get a first win since the 5-0 hammering of Wimbledon in mid-October.

But when Challinor revealed another key player is now injured, it made a little bit more sense.

With eight of the midweek XI having only kicked off 14 league matches for the Owls – the other three only had a combined 75 – Challinor's teamsheet was an act of surrender. Picking your battles, he would say.

Louis Poland and substitute James Kay made debuts, and there was a first start to Denny Oliver.

Connal Trueman made some saves to put minds at rest if Joe Lumley is not fit on Saturday – that seems touch and go –and Oliver and winger Samuel Duruh showed flashes, but no one cast doubt on Challinor's best team, even with all the injuries.

Striker George Brown's first outing of an injury-hit 2026 was a fillip, but after 45 minutes of a fairly dead Trophy game, not a solution.

"It's not been that useful," said Challinor, in reference to the results when asked how helpful starting with two cup games was, "but it's given us a chance to see people.

"We wanted to progress on Sunday (in the FA Cup first round but) we were probably not going to win the FA Cup this season and we're definitely not going to win it now.

"We used it to look at things, but also try and protect some players. That didn't work in some instances. Progression in the (Trophy) allowed us to prioritise Saturday.

"I suppose (Wednesday's game was) what I expected, really.

"Some young players made their debuts and it was a really proud moment for them. They should be better for the experience whether it's good or bad."

The game felt like an obligation to tick off on a freezing night when only 5,472 supporters were in attendance. Fans can be cold on the Trophy, defiled by Premier League under-21 teams, at the best of times. Some take a club of Wednesday's stature having to field their first team in it as an insult.

Depending who they select at the weekend, the Owls could be fined for Wednesday’s weak team. Even if their mitigation does not wash, the punishment will be small, £5,000, but this is a club forced to count the pennies as it emerges from the wreckage left by Dejphon Chansiri.

So what was Challinor protecting them from?

"We've got six or seven players out," he said. "We've got four on international duty. We're coming into a run of fixtures between now and the new year of 11 games so we're going to need all of our players."

Liam Cooper, Billy Mitchell and Louis Barry had trained at the start of the week but not risked. Erine Weaver was.

"Ernie is struggling on the back of the foot injury he had last season," revealed Challinor.

"He's probably got into a rhythm where he plays games and then misses a few days' training to let his foot settle down a bit.

"I thought in the second half he did really well apart from the one mistake where he jumped in and then we concede the (third) goal as a consequence."

Oldham Athletic winning after extra-time on Sunday took a toll.

"Dish (Di'Shon Bernard) was like a tin man on Monday, Tuesday," said his manager. "Jammer (Jamal Lowe), Davo (Davis Keillor-Dunn) had a bit of cramp, Yan (Valery) came off with some cramp. Ash (Maynard-Brewer) got a bit of a whack. He's fine, he probably misses the weekend."

"Max (Lowe) has got a recurrence of the injury he had earlier in the season, so he's going to be out for probably four to six weeks."

Left-sided defender is a key player, especially with Reece James out too.

"It’s disappointing because you saw the impact and profile of him in terms of what we want to try and do in possession,” added Challinor, "but something we'll have to deal with."

So was a proud club surrendering a game, even one of this low priority.

Now Challinor needs Saturday’s end to justify the means.

#1950. Bruno Fernandes has already revealed his dream moves after leaving Manchester United

Bruno Fernandes has already outlined his top three destinations for when he leaves Manchester United.

Fernandes was close to a Man United exit - and moving to Saudi Arabia - during the summer of 2025 when Al-Hilal were understood to be willing to pay £100million for his services and offering the midfielder wages of up to £700,000 a week.

“I would like to experience the Spanish league and fight for big titles in Italy," he told Canal 11 last year. "I have many connections to Italy… my daughter was born there.

#1948. Who can England face in Nations League quarter-final? Next opponents confirmed ahead of Spain showdown

England are on course to record their best ever performance in the Nations League, having qualified for the quarter-finals with victory over Croatia.

Including its inaugural season in 2018/19, the Three Lions have competed in every single Nations League campaign, experiencing some highs and the lowest of lows.

From topping their group and qualifying for the Nations League finals and finishing third to suffering a shock relegation in 2022/23 and then immediate promotion, England have done almost everything except win the competition.

Having started the 2026/27 campaign with a loss to Spain, despite leading 2-1 at one stage, England bounced back in style by beating the Czechs twice and then thumping Croatia 7-0 in a remarkable, record-breaking rout.

Another win over Croatia followed at Wembley on Thursday night to confirm a top-two finish in the group and qualify for the Nations League knockout stage.

England now face a one-game shootout with Spain to decide who will win the group, and an easier quarter-final tie next March.

The four group winners will face the four runners-up in a two-legged Nations League quarter-final.

The group winners will all be seeded and will have home advantage in their respective second leg ties. Teams from the same group cannot be paired together in the knockout stage, therefore England and Spain - for example - would be kept apart.

As things stand, if England finish second in Group 3, their potential Nations League quarter-final opponents would be Italy, Netherlands or Portugal.

Topping the group would set up a possible quarter-final showdown with France, Greece or Denmark.

The draw for the 2026/27 Nations League quarter-final will take place on Friday, November 20 with the ties scheduled to take place in March 2027.

#1946. Scotland are failing to dispel emperor’s new clothes concerns after laboured victory

The Scottish Football Association’s ticket promotion drive for this match emphasised that games are always better under the lights. They might need to re-think that one.

This was another endurance test that at least had a satisfactory outcome, courtesy of John McGinn’s double. In between times a goal for North Macedonia - their first in nine games - probably triggered a national holiday back home and made things look very difficult indeed for Sebastien Pocognoli.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Scotland held onto their lead, given to them after McGinn drove into the box following strong centre-forward play from Che Adams, for the best part of three minutes.

A penalty, awarded after a VAR check a good couple of minutes after goalkeeper Stole Dimitrievski's trip on Ben Gannon-Doak occurred, saved Scotland’s blushes with 16 minutes left and kept their Nations League hopes just about alive.

McGinn did the necessary from the spot although Oli McBurnie, who had replaced Adams six minutes earlier, might have appreciated being given the ball in his seemingly eternal quest for an international goal. It was perhaps too important a kick to take any chances. A manager’s future prospects might have rested on it.

It was a case of third time lucky for Pocognoli as he secured his first Hampden win on what had not seemed like a particularly auspicious date. For the first time since the notorious 0-0 draw against Uruguay that torpedoed their 1986 World Cup, Scotland were in action on a Friday the 13th. What could possibly go wrong? A lot, it seemed at times.

If anything underlined that these are very different times for Scotland it was the sight of Scott McTominay, almost a year to the day since that overhead kick against Denmark, launching himself into the air again in an effort to meet Gilmour’s cross. Although he connected well, the direction was lacking. The ball went high over the bar.

There was no goal from the halfway line this time either. Instead, we were treated to one of the worst misses ever seen at Hampden when Gilmour skied the ball from seven yards seconds after the interval.

The Hampden crowd was getting testy. Boos had greeted the half-time whistle, with the score still goalless and the hosts perhaps lucky not to have conceded.

McGinn’s opener ten minutes after half-time seemed like just the medicine. However, underlining how this was never straightforward, Macedonia equalised almost immediately. They had to score a goal sometime but it was not a good look for Scotland or McTominay, who was beaten in the air at the front post by Elmin Rastodar following a corner.

A clumsy challenge at the other end by Dimitrievski on Gannon-Doak, whose poor touch had already looked to have taken the chance away from him, gave Scotland the gratifying chance to equalise from the spot 17 minutes later.

The hosts had endured an uncertain start that was a decent indicator of what lay ahead. What seemed like teething problems might have been attributed to a defence playing together for the first time. Ryan Porteous was brought back into the starting line-up, his first start since the opening match of Euro 2024 when he was sent off.

Luke Graham, meanwhile, earned his second cap - a first start for Scotland - and was planted right in the middle of the three-man backline. After surviving a few shaky moments initially, the Stoke City defender acquitted himself superbly well.

North Macedonia’s dismal run, which included not having scored in this Nations League campaign so far, perhaps convinced Pocognoli he could make such alterations though injury had restricted his options. Poertoeus, though, hadn’t even been named in the original squad.

Defence wasn’t expected to be an issue. It was a Friday night after a long week at work. Fans wanted to be entertained, they wanted to see some tangible evidence of a new Scotland they have been promised. Pocognoli might wear a suit very well but he’s not proved himself to be his predecessor’s equal at obtaining results, although this was more like it. The fear is that this supposedly more free-flowing Scotland has made them blunter. The phrase the emperor’s new clothes could not be banished from the mind.

Not even McTominay could ignite things. He seemed ready to burst the net just a few minutes later after Lewis Ferguson’s header found the Napoli midfielder with his back to goal in the box. When he turned, it looked like there would be only one outcome. However, Dimitrievski made a tremendous save low to his left.

Yes, this was another occasion where the North Macedonian goalkeeper excelled himself, just as he did in Skopje at the start of last month.

Another save, when he plucked a deflected Adams header out from beneath his crossbar, was even better. There were mitigating factors for Scotland failing to make the breakthrough in the opening half.

It might have been worse for the home team. A cute lay-off from Darko Churlinov set up skipper Enis Bardhi, who lashed a left-footed shot into the side-netting. Most of the Hampden crowd feared the ball had gone in. The smattering of North Macedonia fans were beside themselves.

Sadly for them, happily for the vast majority, the rippling effect was due to the ball hitting the wrong side of the net. It might have been marginally offside in any case. Jeers greeted the blowing of the half-time whistle moments later, nonetheless.

Would Scotland come out with a renewed sense of purpose? It seemed so. Adams pounced on a short pass back and cut the ball back while Dimitrievski dithered.

Billy Gilmour is no one’s idea of a prolific goalscorer but even he couldn’t miss from seven yards, goal gaping. He did. Quite incredibly, the ball comfortably cleared the bar. People were referencing Chris Iwelumo, meaning it was one of the worst misses of all time. It was at the right end, certainly. McGinn showed him how to do it, moving level with Hughie Gallacher in third place on 24 goals in the all-time list of goalscorers and ensuring Andy Robertson’s record-equalling 102nd cap would also be the victorious one the skipper deserved.

#1945. Repubblica: Milan and Real Madrid watching as Napoli star McTominay stalls on contract

Scott McTominay’s Napoli future is in doubt, and a report has named AC Milan among the surprise potential suitors.

In a Napoli side that appears to have lost its way, one of the few lights leading the way remains McTominay. Despite a season that started on the wrong foot and a heart condition (now resolved), the Scot has five goals in 11 games this season across Serie A and the Champions League.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Massimiliano Allegri’s team is going through a tough time, and the former Manchester United player himself has had some tough nights. As La Repubblica (via Calciomercato.com) report, Napoli fans are beginning to worry about where things are heading.

The 29-year-old McTominay is at a turning point in his career, one which has been revitalised since his arrival at Napoli and the Scudetto won under Antonio Conte. His current contract with the Neapolitans expires in 2028, but negotiations for a renewal have stalled.

Fabrizio Romano reported that Napoli remain confident in the possibility of reaching an agreement over an extension, but the uncertainty currently surrounding the project, the bad results and doubts about the club’s future are forcing him to evaluate.

La Repubblica add that the discussions have even stalled after positive steps were taken in September. McTominay and his representatives want to better understand the Azzurri’s vision moving forward before finalising a new agreement.

Sky Switzerland journalist Sacho Tavolieri reported that the former Manchester United man’s agent has already held discussions with several English clubs. Napoli have not completely ruled out a possible sale, and the figure would be €25-30m.

His contract is currently worth €4.5m net per season. Napoli would like to extend it until 2030 with a salary increase, but they are unwilling to accept the Scotsman’s demands, who has requested around €7-8m net per season.

According to La Repubblica, at the end of the season McTominay and Napoli will sit down to discuss the terms of the new contract, once the club’s plans are clearer. Several clubs are interested though and are watching closely.

Aston Villa and Manchester United enquired in the summer. In the coming weeks, Real Madrid and AC Milan will also be keeping a close eye on the developments surrounding McTominay.

#1943. Why Steve McClaren's bad experiences can be good for Rotherham United's Alex Bruce

At other clubs, Bruce might have been shown the door by now, with the Millers only above the League Two trapdoor on goals scored, having played a game more than 23rd-placed Colchester United.

But his fate is effectively in the hands of McClaren, owner Tony Stewart's sounding board.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

The York-born former England manager knows the scale of upheaval at the New York Stadium this summer, and also the value of a bit of patience.

He lost his first four matches as a manager in 2001, and ended the year with Middlesbrough only out of the Premier League relegation zone on goal difference, yet left as their most successful boss.

"I've been through this so many times and if you want a career in management, get used to it," he says. "It doesn't go away.

"Very few times I've been into a football club and it's been easy the first three months. It's not.

"We see that in politics. The first 100 days are difficult.

"He (Bruce) is lucky he's got good experience around him to tell him to shut up moaning in your messages to the players. That's the message to the players – shut up whingeing.

"I've kind of got to be the truth teller to say that's no excuse, we should be doing that better."

And in a different way, he has to be Stewart's truth-teller too.

"I said to him, when you're at the top, you have to be the calm one," says McClaren. "Under the water you might be flapping but it's staying calm and composed, having a plan, sticking to the plan and making sure you fulfil it.

"In the meantime get through the bad times as best you can, stick together and believe in your own ability.”

#1941. Manchester United: How Mauricio Pochettino will differ tactically from Michael Carrick

The Manchester United squad might want to brace themselves for what is coming their way.

Michael Carrick has been sacked and it is expected that Mauricio Pochettino will be arriving to replace him in the Old Trafford dugout.

Pochettino interviewed for the United job in 2024. He was close to getting it on more than one occasion in the years before that too.

Finally he is set to get his chance and the task is now bigger than ever, with United sitting in the relegation zone and in desperate need of a dramatic turnaround.

It is likely to start with hard work. United rank 19th for distance covered in the Premier League this season, with the team set up in a very passive manner.

Fitness has been a concern. When asked in the summer if pre-season had involved a lot of running, Youri Tielemans replied: “No. When you come back from the World Cup, you don’t do lots of running. Just chill.”

There is not going to be much chill with Pochettino around. He has a long history of getting his players working hard.

In the 2013-14 season, his Southampton side covered more distance than any Premier League team. That season, Tottenham ranked 20th.

There is not going to be much chill with Pochettino around

When Pochettino then took over at Spurs the following year, nobody ran further than them over the next four seasons.

That continued at Stamford Bridge. Pochettino’s Chelsea team ranked in the top 10% for all Premier League teams since the 2023-24 season for high turnovers.

The Blues averaged nine high turnovers a match. United are at just over six this season in that metric, and are one of only four teams in the league not to score a goal leading from a high turnover.

It might be a case of being careful what you wish for from a United perspective. After the heavy defeat to Como, Fernandes took aim at Carrick’s back-foot approach.

Art After Dark is back with an exciting calendar of cultural events

“It’s a decision from the staff to not press man-to-man,” Fernandes said. “But sometimes when you give too much of the ball to these teams, they get confidence. They have so many bodies behind the ball that make you run a lot, make people frustrated.

“I think sometimes we have to be more brave under pressure, take the risk of pressing high and making them uncomfortable.”

The high intensity tactical approach that United are expected to deploy under Pochettino draws into focus comments made by Sir Jim Ratcliffe in 2024.

“We’ll decide that [playing] style, plus the CEO, sporting director, probably the recruitment guys,” Ratcliffe said.

“What the style of football is, and that will be the Manchester United style of football, and the coach will have to play that style.

“We’re not going to oscillate from a [Jose] Mourinho style to a [Pep] Guardiola style. That’s not the way we’ll run the club.

“Otherwise, you’re changing everything all the time. You change your coach, you’ve got the wrong squad. We won’t do that.”

What the style of football is, and that will be the Manchester United style of football, and the coach will have to play that style

That is exactly what United have done. From Erik ten Hag they pivoted dramatically to Ruben Amorim and his insistence on a back-three system.

Carrick came in and changed that style again to a lower intensity possession approach, and now it will be all-action under Pochettino. The summer signings of Youri Tielemans and Andrey Santos do not appear to be good fits.

The Argentine will demand legs in midfield and that should be good news for Carlos Baleba, who should have a key role to play.

In defence, Pochettino will want a high defensive line to support the press but that will be a test with the resources at his disposal.

This is a team with the third-worst defensive record in the league and Pochettino must immediately address that.

Harry Maguire and Matthijs de Ligt are much more comfortable defending their own box, meaning the mobility of Leny Yoro and Ayden Heaven could lead to them getting plenty of minutes.

It could be a big opportunity for Patrick Dorgu, too. Pochettino wants full-backs to hold their width, getting up and down the touchline and and allowing the wingers to cut inside.

Dorgu has the engine to do that. He has started only one league match at left-back this season but could become crucial under Pochettino, particularly if it unlocks Matheus Cunha further up the pitch.

Pochettino does not have the luxury of a pre-season. Whipping his players into shape during a campaign will not be easy. However, if he is to get the bounce in results and performances that are sorely needed, it feels essential.

#1940. Sebastien Pocognoli predicts another Scotland record will be broken and identifies ‘something we need to fix’

Sebastien Pocognoli believes it is only a matter of time until John McGinn becomes Scotland’s all-time top goalscorer.

The Scotland manager saw McGinn score a match-winning double to help Scotland secure a scratchy and often uninspired win over North Macedonia. It handed Pocognoli his first Hampden victory at the third attempt and brought some relief for the Belgian.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

It hadn’t looked good when North Macedonia equalised almost immediately after McGinn had put Scotland ahead after 54 minutes. The header from Elmin Rastoder was the visitors' first goal in nine games.

A penalty from McGinn following a VAR check with 16 minutes left, after goalkeeper Stole Dimitrievski clumsily tripped Ben Gannon-Doak, secured the three points for Scotland and kept their hopes of finishing second in their Nations League group alive. Slovenia drew 0-0 with group winners Switzerland.

Pocognoli’s side must win against Switzerland in St Gallen on Monday and hope Macedonia take something from their clash at home against the Slovenians.

With McGinn in the side, anything is possible against Switzerland. Pocognoli hailed the Aston Villa’s contribution and feels he will shortly overtake Kenny Dalglish and Denis Law in the rankings. Both legends scored 30 goals for Scotland and McGinn, who now sits third with Hughie Gallacher on 24 goals, is now just seven goals from overtaking the pair at the top. He has already scored three goals under Pocognoli, having struck a penalty in the 2-0 win against North Macedonia in Skopje last month.

“I'm more focused on the collective challenge and goals,” said Pocognoli. “And I believe if we can build something nice around the collective, then John will one day break the record. He has had a lot of chances through these five games together already. It's important but the individual record I always bring in the collective package. And I hope for him that he can reach it.”

Pocognoli, if not satisfied with all aspects of Scotland’s play, was happy to end the week “with a good feeling” and before travelling to face Switzerland.

He added: “It was not always perfect, but I know that what we worked in two days (this week) happened many times today on the pitch. That's for me very important. On top of that, we created a lot of chances that we really have to score and maybe have a better feeling after the game. But on the whole, I think we were quite aggressive.”

Billy Gilmour missed an open goal shortly after half-time while Dimitrievski pulled off a number of good saves.

“Off the ball, I think we were quite aggressive,” said Pocognoli, who handed a full debut to Stoke City’s Luke Graham in the centre of a three-man defence. “We recover a number of balls that we managed well in some moments of transition.

"We created a big chance for Billy [Gilmour] from this also. So that's a new approach of the game. I think we started the game not that intensely because we didn't manage the ball well. And then for sure you start the game with the feeling that we don't control the ball. After 10 minutes we started to reach Lewis [Ferguson] and Billy [Gilmour] through the lines. And then the game became what we expected.

‘We created chances, we isolated Ben [Gannon-Doak] in the one v one, and we had a lot of pressure. After the first goal I think we need to learn not to drop the intensity. Because after the first goal for 5 minutes I really feel like we dropped the intensity and the focus.

“And we had the same feeling after the second one. So, it's something that we need to fix.”

He agreed Scotland need to be more clinical. “Yes, probably,” he said, while perhaps recalling the missed chances against Slovenia in his first match in charge and which now seem so significant.

‘But I prefer to talk about creating a lot of chances,” he added. “And probably we should keep a clean sheet. So that's really the critical aspect and the demanding aspect. But it's part of the challenge and we are early in the challenge to try to fix this for the future.”

#1938. Barnsley FC's worrying second-half numbers which must change for Daniel Stendel

‘When you have the answer, you can call me every day,’ the Reds head coach replied when The Yorkshire Post tabled the question.

Amid the positivity of two morale-boosting victories in the FA Cup and EFL Trophy – against Oldham Athletic and Aldershot respectively – that nagging second-half issue still persists.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

The Reds shipped two goals apiece after the interval in both games. While the 5-2 and 7-2 scorelines didn't take too much gloss off the wins, the pattern remains a tad annoying.

It continued a worrying trend. The last eight goals that Barnsley have conceded in cup matches have all arrived following the break.

While their recent concessions did not cost them, the story is different at league level, which helps explain Barnsley's position in League One.

Ahead of Saturday’s crunch trip to fellow strugglers Wigan Athletic, the Reds sit second-from-bottom, with their hosts occupying the final spot in the relegation zone.

Barnsley have let in a creditable six goals in the first half of league games in 2026-27. The figure almost triples on the resumption.

The Reds' goal has been breached 16 times in the second period – only Bromley (17) has a worse third-tier record.

Stendel, inset, who is hopeful that the narrative changes with more plentiful options at his disposal in comparison to earlier this autumn said: "I know that we have conceded more in the second half.

“It's not only the defence, it's also the offence. Maybe in the past, we played five games in a row and played with a similar squad in every game. Maybe that’s a reason for it.

"Why can't we do it in the second half when we can do it in the first half? I think fitness is not a problem. I think we're one of the fittest teams in this league.

"I can see it every week in training. It's key that we defend for 90 minutes like most of the time in the first half. When we do it, I think we have a big chance to win a lot of games."

Relative defensive inexperience at this level – which will hopefully improve sooner rather than later – and lapses in concentration are two obvious reasons explaining this.

In what could well be a tense afternoon in Lancashire on Saturday, staying strong for the entire game could prove the difference.

In the EFL Cup tie between these two Roses rivals in August, Barnsley did that in fairness, scoring an equaliser in the final quarter, courtesy of Cameron McGeehan, before progressing on penalties.

A key late goal in their favour on Saturday could be far more important in terms of their season’s narrative.

Stendel added: "It’s more pressure maybe than in our situation normally, but it doesn't matter, it's one game.

"Pressure is part of football, but we need also a little bit of calm to play our game. We're looking forward to it. We're in good shape and in a positive momentum."

#1937. Manchester United dressing room reacts to Michael Carrick sacking

Bruno Fernandes is among the Manchester United players who have paid tribute to Michael Carrick following his sacking.

Carrick arrived at Carrington on Thursday morning and was informed of the decision to relieve him of his duties by Omar Berrada, the club’s chief executive.

“Manchester United can confirm that Michael Carrick has departed his role as men’s first-team head coach,” a statement read.

“Michael rejoined the club in January and guided the team to a third-placed Premier League finish by winning 12 out of the remaining 17 games of the 2025/26 season, accumulating the highest points tally in the league during that period.

“After a disappointing start to the season, the club has come to the extremely difficult conclusion that a change is necessary in order to achieve our ambitions.

“Michael is, and always will be, a Manchester United legend. Just as he did as a player, he has conducted himself with the highest standards of dedication and professionalism throughout his time back with the club.

“His leadership and achievements last season will always be fondly remembered.

“The club intends to appoint a permanent successor as quickly as possible.”

Despite overseeing just one win from the opening 10 Premier League matches of the season and leaving United in the relegation zone, the reaction from some Man United players on social media have proven just how much a popular figure Carrick was in the dressing room.

On Instagram, Fernandes wrote: “Thanks for everything boss”, while Kobbie Mainoo - whose career was rejuvenated by Carrick - posted the exact same words.

There have also been comments from Harry Maguire, Bryan Mbeumo, Patrick Dorgu, Joshua Zirkzee, Ayden Heaven, Tyler Fletcher and Shea Lacey - whom Carrick handed a senior debut earlier this season.

Mauricio Pochettino has been lined up as Carrick’s replacement and is expected to take charge of Man United for their first match back after the international break, when they face Liverpool at Anfield.

According to reports, Pochettino has agreed a two-and-a-half-year contract to become the new Man United manager, with an official announcement imminent.

#1935. Nations League permutations: What England need against Spain to qualify for quarter-finals as group winners

England face Spain this weekend in a Nations League shootout to decide who tops Group A3.

Victory over Croatia on Thursday evening meant England officially joined Spain in qualifying for the Nations League knockout phase with a game to spare.

Though, as things stand, the reigning world and European champions lead the way with a three-point lead over England - courtesy of their victory at Wembley Stadium during the autumn international break.

Since then, La Roja have beaten Croatia and the Czech Republic twice each and just need to avoid defeat against Three Lions in the reverse fixture on Sunday to guarantee top spot and an easier quarter-final draw.

However, as England have the superior goal difference (+12 compared to +9) between the two nations, a win for Thomas Tuchel’s side in Madrid would be enough to see them top the group at Spain’s expense.

This is because the UEFA tiebreaker first looks at the head-to-head record when sides are locked on the same amount of points, and then total goal difference in the two games between the two sides.

As Spain won the reverse fixture by a one-goal margin in September, any margin of victory for England - whether it be 1-0, 2-0 or 2-1 - will guarantee top spot in Nations League Group A3.

Topping the group would set up a possible quarter-final showdown with France, Greece or Denmark, as things currently stand.

Furthermore, the group winners will be seeded for the Nations League quarter-final draw, therefore securing home advantage in their second leg ties.

Teams from the same group cannot be paired together in the knockout stage, therefore England and Spain - for example - would be kept apart.

Were England to fail to beat Spain and finish second in Group 3, their potential Nations League quarter-final opponents would be Italy, Netherlands or Portugal.

#1933. When will Mauricio Pochettino start as Manchester United manager?

Mauricio Pochettino now knows when he will begin work as Manchester United manager, following Michael Carrick ‘s sacking on Thursday.

The Red Devils parted company with the former midfielder after a run of one win in 11 games in all competitions, with the club mired in the Premier League relegation zone and 17th in the Champions League table.

Former Tottenham and Chelsea boss Pochettino has been sounded out as INEOS’ preferred candidate, ahead of other potential options that were previously reported, like Eddie Howe, Antonio Conte and Julian Nagelsmann, and has agreed a two-and-a-half-year contract to replace Carrick

Pochettino will not come cheap, though, with United triggering the £7million clause in his contract with US Soccer to bring him to Old Trafford.

But, when will Pochettino start work as manager?

The slight spanner in the works is the USMNT games games Haiti on Saturday and Tuesday evening.

However, Man Utd have confirmed that Pochettino will stay to oversee the double-header before starting work at Old Trafford mere hours later on Wednesday, November 18.

That would give the Argentine just a few training sessions with his new players before his first match in charge – the Premier League trip to Liverpool on Sunday, November 22.

Pochettino is expected to bring four members of his backroom staff with him to Manchester as he prepares for a return to English football.

#1932. Manchester City, Chelsea, Tottenham... Premier League clubs battle for Lens ‘new Varane’

By Axel Clody | 12 Nov 2026 06:48

Lens centre-back Ismaelo Ganiou, tipped for a big-money sale in the summer of 2027, is seeing the list of his suitors grow a few months ahead of the next transfer windows.

Lens, who are looking for a new manager to replace Yannick Cahuzac, are enduring a difficult 2026-27 season so far. It is a campaign that could (should) be the last for centre-back Ismaelo Ganiou.

Kept in the squad until the end of the 2026 summer transfer window, the 21-year-old French prospect now has a strong chance of leaving. Lens are probably already thinking about a huge sale for a player who could break into the top 10 biggest sales in the northern French club’s history.

Now the most highly valued player in the squad on the transfer market, with an estimated market value of £25.5m (€30m), level with French goalkeeper Robin Risser, Ganiou has seen his value rise by £8.5m (€10m) between June and September 2026, a sign of his rapid progress.

His current absence, estimated at several weeks because of a knee injury, does nothing to change the trend of a growing number of clubs taking an interest in his situation and profile.

The list is a long one, with no fewer than 11 clubs reported to be in the running to date.

In France, two other suitors in Ligue 1 have joined Paris Saint-Germain, namely Marseille and Monaco.

Those three French clubs face competition from six Premier League sides for a player regarded as the ‘new Varane’, a reference to the fact that the future 2018 world champion left Lens for Real Madrid in the summer of 2011, before moving to Manchester United ten years later.

Manchester City, Chelsea, Tottenham, Newcastle, Fulham and Brentford are the English clubs named in this case. In Italy, Atalanta and Como, who recently beat Lens at Bollaert-Delelis (9-1), are the two Serie A sides interested. Borussia Dortmund and RB Leipzig of Germany are also monitoring a situation that is far from having reached a verdict.

It is fair to say that Ganiou’s summer 2027 transfer window promises to be particularly lively. With no fewer than 13 suitors already named, the young defender is attracting growing interest on the European market, which promises some fine battles between several clubs keen to secure his services.

It remains to be seen whether Lens will manage to keep hold of their gem or whether one of these clubs will make a concrete move in the coming months.

#1930. Leeds United icon and ex-Middlesbrough man Jonathan Woodgate follows Michael Carrick out of Manchester United

Former Leeds United and Middlesbrough star Jonathan Woodgate has followed Michael Carrick out of the door at Manchester United.

The 46-year-old is a familiar face in Yorkshire having made over 100 appearances for both Leeds and Middlesbrough.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

He established himself among Europe’s most exciting young talents during his Leeds days and later had three spells on the books at Middlesbrough.

Woodgate also had a spell as Middlesbrough boss and was a first-team coach during Carrick’s reign at the Riverside.

The pair were reunited at Old Trafford in January, but has now departed in the wake of Carrick’s dismissal.

As reported by the BBC, Woodgate has moved on along with fellow coaches Steve Holland, Jonny Evans, Travis Binnion and Craig Mawson.

Reports have indicated USA head coach and ex-Tottenham Hotspur boss Mauricio Pochettino is being lined up to take the Red Devils reins.

A club statement confirming Carrick’s exit read: “Manchester United can confirm that Michael Carrick has departed his role as men’s first-team head coach.

“Michael rejoined the club in January and guided the team to a third-placed Premier League finish by winning 12 out of the remaining 17 games of the 2025/26 season, accumulating the highest points tally in the league during that period.

“After a disappointing start to the season, the club has come to the extremely difficult conclusion that a change is necessary in order to achieve our ambitions.

“Michael is, and always will be, a Manchester United legend. Just as he did as a player, he has conducted himself with the highest standards of dedication and professionalism throughout his time back with the club. His leadership and achievements last season will always be fondly remembered.

“The club intends to appoint a permanent successor as quickly as possible.”

#1929. Mauricio Pochettino to Manchester United: Key lessons from his time at Chelsea

By Axel Clody | 12 Nov 2026 07:07

Mauricio Pochettino’s time at Chelsea left a series of lessons that Manchester United must consider before handing the Argentine responsibility for running their sporting project.

More than the results he achieved at Stamford Bridge, the manager’s experience in London exposed difficulties that go beyond what a manager can do on the touchline, and help explain why the choice of a manager, on its own, does not solve a club’s problems.

Pochettino finished the 2023-24 season with Chelsea in sixth place in the Premier League, after an uneven start and a consistent recovery in the closing stages. There were five consecutive wins in the final matches, as well as a League Cup runners-up finish and an FA Cup semi-final. The performance pointed to progress, but it was not enough to secure his future.

His exit, announced by mutual consent, highlighted differences over sporting planning and raised a question that also concerns United: to what extent can a manager develop his work when structural decisions are not moving in the same direction?

The possible arrival of Mauricio Pochettino at Manchester United carries a particularity that makes his Chelsea spell even more relevant. If the deal goes through, the Argentine will not take over a team at the start of a new cycle, with time for a pre-season, involvement in building the squad and gradual implementation of his ideas.

He will find a club in 18th place in the Premier League after ten matches, in a situation that demands an immediate reaction to avoid the threat of relegation and climb the table.

The scenario places Pochettino before two simultaneous responsibilities: restoring Manchester United competitively and starting to build a project that is not limited to an emergency solution. What does his experience at Chelsea teach about that balance?

At Stamford Bridge, the Argentine faced planning difficulties, worked with a deeply overhauled squad and managed to bring about a sporting recovery that, although significant, did not secure his stay.

Pochettino’s Chelsea finished the 2023-24 season in a sporting condition different from the one shown in the early matches.

The recovery in the Premier League, the run of five consecutive wins and the attacking output of 77 goals indicated important progress. On the other hand, the 63 goals conceded exposed a fragility that prevented the team from reaching greater consistency.

That trajectory highlights the challenge the Argentine will face in Manchester. At Chelsea, the improvement came over a full season. At United, the margin for a gradual recovery is considerably smaller. The team is in the relegation zone, and every match without a win increases the pressure on the manager and the players.

Before establishing a fully developed style of play, Pochettino will need to restore competitiveness to a group going through a sporting crisis.

That does not mean abandoning the construction of a football model in favour of immediate results. On the contrary, United will need to find a way to reconcile the two. Improving defensive organisation, establishing pressing patterns and restoring the players’ confidence are measures that can produce effects in both the short and the long term.

Assessing the work, in this context, also requires care. The league position will be decisive at first, but it cannot be the only criterion for measuring progress. The ability to control matches, reduce errors and develop players must accompany the recovery in results.

Pochettino has a record of building competitive teams, as he showed at Tottenham, Premier League runners-up in 2016-17 and Champions League finalists in 2019. Even so, the Manchester context will demand a much more immediate response than the one he had in London.

Pochettino’s exit from Chelsea, after a significant improvement in the closing stages, is perhaps the most relevant aspect of his experience at Stamford Bridge.

The Argentine finished the Premier League in sixth place but left the club in May 2024. Differences over sporting planning and the running of the project were among the factors cited for the end of the relationship.

The episode showed that improvement on the pitch, on its own, does not guarantee continuity. A manager can revive a team, develop players and improve results, but still depend on a structure that shares his priorities and provides the conditions to sustain the work.

Manchester United must consider this aspect from day one. The club’s sporting structure, with those responsible for planning and recruitment, must work in tune with Pochettino. That does not mean concentrating every decision in the manager’s hands, but establishing in advance the transfer priorities, the sporting objectives and the limits of each professional’s remit.

The difficulty will be even greater because the manager will arrive mid-season, under pressure for results and with little room to correct structural problems. If United demand an immediate recovery but do not provide the conditions to reorganise the squad and implement his ideas, they risk repeating the cycle they intend to break.

His time at Chelsea does not invalidate Pochettino’s work. On the contrary, the team’s recovery and the performance of players under his management offer arguments in favour of the appointment. But they also show that there is a difference between improving a team and building a project capable of remaining competitive.

At Old Trafford, that distinction will be decisive. Pochettino will first need to move Manchester United away from the relegation zone, but the club cannot allow urgency to turn the work into a series of short-term decisions.

#1928. Manchester United: Mauricio Pochettino appointed manager on two-and-a-half year deal

Manchester United have confirmed the appointment of Mauricio Pochettino as head coach, as he replaces Michael Carrick.

Pochettino has signed a two-and-a-half year deal at Old Trafford, marking his fourth stint in English football following spells with Southampton, Tottenham and Chelsea.

The Argentine succeeds Carrick - who was sacked on Thursday - after overseeing a disappointing start to the Premier League season, with Man United sitting in the relegation zone after winning just one of their opening 10 matches.

Pochettino, however, will not start work as Man Utd boss straight away as he is set to continue in his role as USMNT manager for their CONCACAF Nations League two-legged quarter-final against Haiti.

That said, the appointment does mean Pochettino will be in the dugout at Anfield next Sunday to take charge of his first Man United game against bitter rivals Liverpool.

“Mauricio Pochettino has agreed to become the Manchester United men’s head coach from 18 November,” a statement reads.

“The club has reached an agreement with the U.S. Soccer Federation for Mauricio and his staff to be released after the conclusion of their responsibilities with the U.S. Men’s National Team.

“The Argentinian is renowned for his high-intensity, attacking style of football, his dedication to building strong, cohesive teams and his outstanding record of developing individual players.

“Pochettino has consistently performed at the highest level of football across multiple leagues. He began his coaching career with Espanyol in 2009 before joining Southampton and achieving a club-record Premier League points tally in 2014.

“During five full seasons at Tottenham Hotspur, Pochettino established the club as regular UEFA Champions League contenders, securing qualification in four consecutive seasons and leading the club to its first final in the competition in 2019.

#1927. ‘Not ready’, ‘out of control’ and ‘the end of the world’: What Amorim’s words tell us about Milan’s state

Ruben Amorim is not one to hold back when it comes to speaking his thoughts to the media, and the last few days are no exception.

The past week or so has seen Amorim have to digest the best and worst of his AC Milan side. The 3-1 derby win over Inter generated a euphoria that begun whispers of the word ‘Scudetto’, before a dismal defeat to Ferencvaros which saw Milan drop to 29th in the Europa League standings.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

This rollercoaster of extremes didn’t stop either side of those two games either. Before the victory over the Nerazzurri a 2-1 lead had been coughed up against Bologna, who scored three times in the second half to win at San Siro and inflict the first league defeat on the Rossoneri.

Yesterday, the Diavolo responded to the season low-point against the Hungarians by beating a Genoa side that had won their last three games and four of their last five. This Milan team is a very difficult one to work out, and it seems even the manager is struggling to do so.

After the Ferencvaros and Genoa games, we learned a lot about where Amorim sees his team to be at. Some key lines from his post-match comments demonstrated a wide spectrum of reaction, from anger to pride, passing through encouragement and worry.

Ruben Amorim has often gone to bat for his players after negative performances and results this season, but it seems that the defeat on Thursday night had pushed his patience to the brink as he tore into his team after the game.

“There’s no explanation. There’s nothing I can say, especially about the first half. I don’t remember another first half like it. It’s about ambition, concentration, desire,” he said.

“We gave away opportunities, we gave away stupid gifts. We weren’t prepared to play football tonight. I usually have a lot to say in defence of our team, but not tonight. We need to be more humble and understand what happened.”

For the first time we saw a peek behind the mask, one that has very often been one portraying an optimistic and positive expression. Amorim knew there was no point attempting to lie to the supporters, the media but above all to himself.

What we know is that Amorim echoed the ferocity of these sentiments when speaking in the dressing room after full-time in what was likely the first dressing down that the team got. Six players were reported to have disappointed more than the others, too.

Above all, what stood out was the fact that the head coach opted to question whether his players wanted it enough. This was no longer a question of learning an identity, rotation or an injury crisis: it became a matter of heart.

Another intriguing extract from the post-Ferencvaros tirade that Amorim went on was about the squad’s ability to balance playing in two different competitions, namely Serie A and the Europa League.

“We’re not ready to be competitive on two fronts. We need to work on our way of looking at football and how we approach matches. There are no excuses tonight, there’s nothing I can say.

“I have to focus on the league, obviously, but we also have to do well in the Europa League. We must and can win games despite the rotation. We have to be ready – we’re not now – to play and win every three days.

“But I won’t give up on this competition. But as long as the mathematics don’t condemn us, we’ll fight in this competition as we do in the others.”

Once again, Amorim offered a bit of a revelation: the league is the absolute priority for Milan this season. It may not exactly be revolutionary information, given that a top four spot remains the most accessible avenue to the main objective for 2026-27: securing a Champions League return.

And yet, in his emotional outburst, the former Sporting CP and Manchester United boss told us all in black and white that Serie A will be the focus. As a result, it’s right to expect more ups and downs in Europe, especially with such a depleted squad.

There is an element of observational realism about Amorim’s words; almost an admission of defeat in his attempts to spin two plates at the same time and get the most out of the resources at his disposal. Does it suggest a Europa League resurgence is coming? Not exactly.

Amorim has not made a habit of mentioning individuals ever since his arrivals, both in his pre-match words but especially after games in which emotions are running high. However, he brought up someone who was absent for the Ferencvaros game.

“Everyone needs to train like Pavlovic. He’s ready to die in training. He’s a good example. Sometimes when players don’t start, they struggle. But there are no excuses, we should have won even with those who started,” he said.

Going into the season there were some who were legitimately questioning whether Strahinja Pavlovic would even be a tactical fit for Amorim’s usual 3-4-2-1 system, given that he prefers more composed, ball-playing outside centre-backs.

The answer to those doubts is that in November the Serbian has become the shining light in the eyes of his manager. We mentioned earlier that it had become a question of heart, and nobody can doubt that Pavlovic has that in abundance.

For all of the talk about tactics, systems, shapes and patterns, football is a simple game that very often comes down to who wants it more. In this regard, Amorim elevated Pavlovic as the example to follow, while hoping he returns from injury for the Frosinone game after the break.

Moving on to the post-Genoa reflections, what was quite apparent was that Ruben Amorim was in no mood to get carried away. In fact, if anything, he revealed his belief that his team are still miles off where he wants them.

“What I feel is that, when we’re competitive, we’re difficult to beat, and now we’re steering the game towards our style. We push for control with the ball.

“When we’re not able to be competitive, we’re completely out of control. It’s a big difference, but it’s something we need to work on. But again, the team’s evolution, the way we’re playing, is completely different from the start of the season, and I’m happy with that.

“We should have more points. I’m clearly not happy with the European games, not just because of the results, but because of the performance. Results can happen, but the performances are far from what we want. However, I think we’ll be a better team in the future.”

So, for now this version of Milan is not one that satisfies the coach. The words are a good summary of what the last six games have shown, in which there have been an even split of victories and defeats: on their day the team can beat anyone in the league, but on an off-day they can lose to anyone too.

What Amorim seems keen to hammer home is that progress for this season will be judged on the ability to bring the ceiling closer to the floor. In other words, we have seen the potential of this team already with some impressive wins, yet the base level for performances remains frighteningly low.

Consistency is not just about being able to string together several positive results in a row, something the current Rossoneri do not seem capable of. It is about the repeated displaying of an idea and an identity every few days, to suggest the team are getting closer to the vision the coach has.

Various things make that difficult (perhaps unachievable, based on Amorim’s other comments) right now, such as the injury situation and the multiple windows needed to sculpt the squad. Progress is not always linear, but the target has been set.

One of the themes that Amorim has been consistently questioned on this season is how to unlock the club-record signing Goncalo Ramos, who remains stuck on three goals (one of which was a penalty).

After the Genoa game, he said: “I think we’re lacking time in the final third. We control the ball away from the opponent’s penalty area. This is also key for Goncalo Ramos to have more clear-cut chances. It’s clearly not Goncalo’s fault.

“Pulisic is far from the penalty area. Gonçalo is far from the penalty area. All these players play away from the penalty area, so I can say we’re still far from the final product, because we’re still working on good progression, but then in the final third of the pitch we waste a lot of time with the ball there.”

This is one of the points of ‘evolution’ that Amorim clearly wants to see from his side, but is yet to achieve. Milan are not yet a team that can sustain pressure in the opposition half, nor can they penetrate the box with any regularity either.

In fact, a report from Sky backed this up with some interesting numbers, look specifically at data per 30 minutes of actual possession. Milan are first in Serie A for build-up actions, but they are 20th for entries into the final third and entries into the opposition box.

Amorim’s side are 19th for percentage of touches in the attacking third and 18th in percentage of touches in the opposition box. When the Rossoneri have the ball, it is rarely in a threatening area.

With numbers like these, there isn’t much for Ramos to get on the end of, and it makes the positive attacking numbers (23 goals in 11 league games) feel quite unsustainable.

The Portuguese striker meanwhile is first in the Milan squad in Serie A for interceptions, recoveries, touches in the middle third and touches in the opposition half. He is second for receptions, touches and duels, and third for passes.

Simply put, the No.9 is being drawn away from the area he should be operating in because the team are not capable of sustaining spells of possession further up the field, so he needs to drop deeper to feel involved.

This is something Amorim must work on, because while the goals are coming from other sources for now – in some cases due to the space Ramos helps create – it could all come tumbling down unless the attacking play improves more generally.

🚨🎙️🛡️ Ruben Amorim on Gonçalo Ramos: “Ramos is helping US more than we are helping him. It’s a TEAM problem, not a Ramos problem.”

“We don’t spend enough time in the final third.”

“When we start keeping the ball there more often, Gonçalo is going to score MANY goals.” pic.twitter.com/b3Zs6YxNym

— Milan Wire (@MilanWireX) November 8, 2026

Finally, we end with what was perhaps the most passionate part of Amorim’s comments following the win at the Stadio Luigi Ferraris on Sunday, again centred around the levels he expects from his team.

“It’s the mentality. When you’re a player, there are no off days. If you play for Milan, for these clubs, there are no off days. You can’t show up like we did on Thursday and then turn it on again for Sunday. It’s not possible, it’s not something that will work.

“It’s not a physical condition, it’s a question of anxiety about defeat. If you ‘panic’ about defeat, it’s not that you’re afraid of losing, but that you know that losing is the end of the world. That’s the feeling I want my teams to have.”

In many ways, the manager was speaking in a way that channels how fans have experienced the past week. How is it possible that Milan can be completely outplayed by a side sat third in the Hungarian lead just days after convincingly beating the Italian champions?

Against Genoa, how can the team play as they did in the first half, and then appear to completely drop off a cliff in the second half when the time came to dig deep and bring the result home? The disparity in levels both in-game and from match to match is astounding everyone, even the man in charge.

What Amorim said about wanting his side to fear losing was particularly poignant. In his time at the club so far he has repeatedly stressed that feeling of responsibility to honour the red and black shirt and all that comes with that, including the importance of results.

Some may argue that encouraging an ‘end of the world’ type mentality will not help the players play more carefree and will actually only stiffen them up. Yet, it could also provide the stimulus for the fight and the courage that Amorim clearly so desperately wants.

There is a hint of irony about the ‘no days off’ comment, as Amorim has given the squad a one-week break, at least those who were not called up by their national teams. When everyone reconvenes there will be another crucial stretch of games to see out the year, starting with a home match against the surprise package Frosinone.

For all of the energy, passion and emotion that Ruben Amorim speaks with, it will eventually be time for words to become deeds. Consistency must be not a distant mirage but some thing tangible that emerges.

Only then will a full buy-in be achieved and patience be awarded. Otherwise there will always be the fear that darkness follows light.

#1926. ‘I’m not afraid to say that’ - James Justin on Leicester City exit and new lease of life at Leeds United

Leeds United defender James Justin has conceded he “wasn’t great” in his final season at Leicester City.

The 28-year-old played in Europe and represented England during his six years at Leicester, but his Foxes spell ended on a sour note.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

He suffered relegation from the Premier League with the club in 2025 and by his own admission, struggled for form during that ill-fated campaign.

When he was snapped up by Leeds for a reported £8m plus £2m in add-ons in August 2025, many Leicester fans were quick to point out his below-par performances.

He told Leeds Live: “I would say I obviously didn't leave Leicester on the best of terms in terms of getting relegated twice in three seasons, and we weren't great that year at all, and I wasn't great that year, I'm not afraid to say that.

“I didn't play to the best of my ability, for whatever reason, I don't know. But it's been a good start here so far.

“I'm grateful that the club had that faith in me and hopefully I've repaid that so far.”

To say Justin has enjoyed a new lease of life at Elland Road would be an understatement. A full-back by trade, he has slotted seamlessly into a central back three with Tarik Muharemović and Nico Elvedi and kept £15m man Jaka Bijol out of the side.

Praise has been lavished upon the Luton Town academy product, but he is not thinking about a recall to the England squad.

He said: “Do I think about an England call-up? Not really. I understand football and the way it goes in terms of England and I feel obviously the man sitting over there (Jayden Bogle), and we've spoken about him before, is due a call-up before I am to be honest.

“He's got a lot of potential. I'd back him as a player to go into that group and perform to the abilities that I know that he's got.

“When that day comes, and I'm sure it will hopefully come soon if we obviously keep it up as a team throughout the season, I'll be cheering his name.

“I feel like he's a top-class player, and especially with the dominant style that England play in the majority of their games, it'd be perfect and definitely be a luxury player in that England team.”

#1924. As well as Luke Shaw: Mauricio Pochettino set for major Man Utd injury boost before Liverpool clash

By Lewis Blain | 12 Nov 2026 07:16

Manchester United could welcome two important players back for their Premier League trip to Liverpool on November 22nd.

Marcus Rashford is working towards a return from a troublesome groin injury, while Luke Shaw is also targeting a comeback after being sidelined since October.

The potential double boost could provide incoming manager Mauricio Pochettino with some welcome options if he takes charge ahead of the Anfield showdown.

According to the Daily Mail, United are hopeful Rashford will be available for the clash against Liverpool after the forward began a new treatment programme.

The 29-year-old returned to Old Trafford in the summer following a season-long loan at Barcelona, but has struggled with a hip problem sustained at the 2026 World Cup.

Rashford featured in United's opening six Premier League matches, as well as their Carabao Cup exit to Brighton & Hove Albion and Champions League defeat to Atletico Madrid in October, before the issue worsened and spread into his groin.

He visited a specialist in Dublin last week alongside a member of United's medical staff, with a fresh recovery programme now in place.

Rashford is said to have wanted to continue supporting Carrick and even offered to make himself available from the bench against Chelsea, but United decided against risking him further.

The forward has an impressive record against Liverpool, scoring seven goals in 20 appearances against United's rivals, and his availability would represent a significant boost.

Shaw is also targeting a return for the trip to Merseyside after suffering a muscle injury against Tottenham Hotspur on October 10th. The left-back has missed seven matches across all competitions.

The potential returns could coincide with a major change in the United dugout, with Carrick expected to be dismissed on Thursday 12th November, and USMNT boss Pochettino lined up to take over.

The Argentine could therefore make his return to Premier League management against Liverpool, having previously managed Spurs, Chelsea and Southampton.

Pochettino would inherit a difficult situation, with United sitting in the relegation zone after a disappointing start to the campaign.

However, having Rashford and potentially Shaw available would give him more options for his first major test, particularly with United needing greater attacking threat and defensive stability.

Neither player's return is guaranteed, but the timing could hardly be better for a new manager preparing for one of the biggest fixtures of the season.

#1923. Manchester United recruitment team should be ‘sacked’ over £50m transfer, says Jamie Redknapp

Jamie Redknapp says Andrey Santos is ‘not a Manchester United player’ and claims whoever was responsible for his signing ‘deserves the sack’.

Desperate for midfield reinforcements over the summer, United spent £50m to sign Brazil international Santos from Premier League rivals Chelsea.

Manchester United made midfield targets their priority after Casemiro left Old Trafford and Manuel Ugarte suffered a serious injury at the World Cup.

Carlos Baleba and Youri Tielemans joined Michael Carrick’s squad on top of Santos but all three midfielders have made inauspicious starts to their United careers.

Santos has earned just seven starts for a Manchester United team sitting in the relegation zone heading into the international break.

Read exclusive analysis of the biggest stories in football with Metro's weekly football newsletter In The Mixer. Sign up now for free.

Redknapp doubts the 22-year-old Brazilian is at the level required to play for United and says bringing him to the club was a ‘sackable offence’ by those in charge at Old Trafford.

‘Can I throw one player at you? And this is no disrespect to the boy, because he’s not a bad player, but whoever brought in Andrey Santos, that for me is a sackable offence,’ Redknapp said on The Overlap Daily, sponsored by Sky Vegas.

‘He is not a Manchester United player. He’s a decent player, he’s okay. But they brought [Youri] Tielemans in just after it.

‘What makes them think, “Okay, I’m going to get two midfield players”, when I’ve got [Kobbie] Mainoo there – three very similar players that haven’t got any athleticism to get round the pitch?’

Use AI to go deeper into the stories you care about – powered by Metro and trusted publications.

When it was point to him that Manchester United’s director of recruitment Christopher Vivell knew Santos from his previous spell at Chelsea, Redknapp added: ‘Even worse, then. I’d let them off the hook if they didn’t know him.’

Liverpool legend Steven Gerrard has also criticised Manchester United’s pursuit of Santos, who made just 47 appearances for Chelsea.

‘I’m not sure Andrey Santos was the right signing for Manchester United at £50m,’ Gerrard said last month.

‘I just think to play in Manchester United’s midfield every single game, every single weekend, you’d expect to compete for the Premier League and the Champions League.

‘Santos, he’s a good player, but for me, he’s not a Manchester United player. I think he’s a bit short, that would be my opinion. United’s midfield is way off the level, it’s way off.’

United’s dismal start to the 2026/27 campaign looks set to cost former England midfielder Carrick his job at Old Trafford.

Mauricio Pochettino, the former Chelsea and Tottenham boss, is the frontrunner to take over at Manchester United.

If appointed, Pochettino’s first game in charge of the Red Devils would be a daunting trip to Anfield to face arch-rivals Liverpool after the international break.

#1922. Spain vs England: Nations League prediction, kick-off time, TV, live stream, team news, h2h results, odds

The Standard's journalism is supported by our readers. If you click links to other sites on this page, we will earn commission.

England and Spain both have eyes on top spot in Nations League A3 ahead of a heavyweight showdown this weekend.

The Three Lions guaranteed themselves a top-two finish after beating Croatia on Thursday, but can still topple the reigning world and European champions.

With five matches played apiece, it all comes down to this. England currently trail Spain by three points, which means only a win will see them qualify for the quarter-finals as group winners by virtue of a superior goal difference.

Spain, who have won their last 12 matches in a row, have the luxury of knowing a point is enough to keep them top and thus secure a, potentially, easier knockout phase route.

Spain vs England is scheduled for a 7.45pm GMT kick-off on Sunday, November 15, 2026.

The match will take place at the Metropolitano Stadium, home of La Liga giants Atletico Madrid.

TV channel: In the UK, Spain vs England in the 2026/27 Nations League is being televised live and free to air on ITV, with coverage of the match beginning at 7pm on ITV1.

Live stream: Catch the game live online through the ITVX website and app, which is free with a registration.

Live blog: You can follow all the action with Standard Sport’s live blog, featuring expert insight and analysis from England correspondent Dom Smith.

England could have Ezri Konsa and Djed Spence available for the showdown in the Spanish capital after the defenders missed the win over Croatia through injury.

Thomas Tuchel said in the pre-Croatia press conference that the pair were due to resume team training on Saturday to be ready for the Spain game.

If fit, Konsa and Spence would be options to replace Trent Alexander-Arnold (thus seeing Jarell Quansah move out to right-back) and Lewis Hall respectively, to provide England with greater defensive security.

The front four could be unchanged from the Croatia game with Harry Kane - winning his 127th senior cap - leading the line ahead of Jude Bellingham, Morgan Rogers and Anthony Gordon.

For Spain, the big concern was Lamine Yamal after the Barcelona star sat out the win over the Czech Republic because of a knee issue.

However, Luis de la Fuente revealed afterwards that Yamal is in “perfect condition” to start and play 90 minutes which should see him replace Yeremy Pino in attack.

The reverse fixture at Wembley Stadium in September was nothing short of a classic as England had their moments in matching the world champions.

Ultimately, Spain’s class proved decisive as they ran out 3-2 winners and, in truth, they would have won by a bigger margin had it not been for some wayward finishing.

Spain are simply in their groove and we cannot see England ending their long unbeaten run.

England did win this very fixture on their last visit to Spain in October 2018 when Raheem Sterling (x2) and Marcus Rashford had them 3-0 up before half-time.

Paco Alcacer and Sergio Ramos reduced the deficit in the second half, but the Three Lions held on for a famous win.
